0.title: Waiting for His Son from Heaven
0.overview:
First Thessalonians is probably the earliest of Paul’s letters preserved in the New Testament — penned from Corinth around AD 50–51, within just weeks or months of his departure from the Thessalonian church. It is a letter warm with affection, urgent with concern, and radiant with hope. More than almost any other letter in the Pauline corpus, it vibrates with the pulse of a young church under pressure and a pastor who loves them like a father, a mother, and a brother all at once.

The city of Thessalonica was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia — a major port, a commercial hub, a city full of every religion Rome and the East could offer. Paul had arrived there on his second missionary journey, preached for perhaps three weeks in the synagogue, and watched as a community of faith was born — Jewish converts, god-fearing Greeks, and not a few prominent women (Acts 17:1–9). Then a riot broke out, the city authorities were alarmed, and Paul was smuggled out by night. He never forgot those he had left behind.

The letter's great themes weave together like threads in a tapestry. There is the gospel — how it arrived in Thessalonica not merely as words but in power, in the Holy Spirit, in full conviction (1:5). There is the church as a community shaped by faith, hope, and love — Paul's great triad appears here earlier than in 1 Corinthians 13. There is holiness — the call to sanctification, especially in the realm of sexual purity, that flies directly in the face of Greco-Roman culture. And there is the return of Christ — the parousia — which dominates the last two chapters and gives the whole letter its eschatological urgency. The Thessalonians were grieving for those who had died before Jesus returned; Paul's answer is the most vivid description of the Second Coming in all of Scripture.

Above all, this is a letter about hope. Not the vague optimism the world calls hope, but the taut, muscular, resurrection-grounded hope that transforms how believers grieve, how they work, how they treat their bodies, and how they face the future. 'We do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep,' Paul writes, 'so that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope' (4:13). That contrast — hope versus hopelessness — is the heartbeat of 1 Thessalonians. The God who raised Jesus will raise them. The Lord who ascended will descend. The church that suffers now will be presented blameless before him at his coming.

1.title: The Gospel That Works
1.overview:
This is probably the earliest letter in the New Testament, written around AD 50 from Corinth. Paul had preached in Thessalonica, capital of Macedonia, for only a few weeks before a riot forced him out by night (Acts 17:1–10). He had been frantic about the young church he left behind, and chapter 1 is his relief and thanksgiving at the news that they are standing.

He thanks God for their faith that works, love that labours and hope that endures. He knows God chose them, because the gospel came to them with the Spirit’s power and changed them. They received it with joy in the middle of persecution, and the story of their conversion has spread across Greece: they turned from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven, Jesus, who rescues us from the coming wrath. Turned, serving, waiting: the whole Christian life in ten verses.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter opens with the names of the three missionaries who founded the church, Paul, Silas and Timothy, and greets the Thessalonian believers as a congregation whose life is rooted in God the Father and the Lord Jesus, wishing them grace and peace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Joining the Father and the Lord Jesus as a single source of grace and peace is a compressed Christology, and its date is what makes it startling. This letter is very likely the earliest document in the New Testament, written around twenty years after the crucifixion — well before any Gospel. There was no long development during which a human teacher was gradually elevated to divine status. The highest view of Christ is already here, in the first line of the first thing written, stated as though it needed no defence.

The Reformed tradition, with Nicaea, has always insisted that a creature cannot be a co-source of divine blessing. Grace and peace come from God; if they come from Jesus in the same breath and under the same preposition, then Jesus is not on the creature side of the line. The greeting is a doxology in miniature: two persons, one blessing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In Thessalonica, kyrios was Caesar's title, and the city was proud of its standing with Rome — a free city that had backed the winning side and kept its own assembly for it. Acts records the charge laid against these believers exactly: they say there is another king, Jesus (Acts 17:7). To receive a letter greeting them from the Lord Jesus was to be reminded whose throne their welfare actually came from.

Now: Notice what Paul does not put in his greeting. No title, no credentials, no reminder of what he had done for them. Where he was loved and trusted he simply used his name. It is a small thing, and it is a fair question for anyone who holds office in a church: how much of your authority do you find you have to keep asserting, and why?

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace to you and peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace to you and peace.

Meaning first. 1 Thessalonians is one of Paul’s earliest letters, written to a young church that had been planted in a few weeks and then left suddenly under persecution. Paul writes to encourage them, to answer slanders against him, to teach them holiness, and to comfort them about believers who had died before Christ’s return. Chapter 1 is a thanksgiving. Paul remembers their work of faith, labour of love and steadfastness of hope (vv. 1–3). He knows God chose them, because the gospel came to them not only in words but with power, the Holy Spirit and deep conviction (vv. 4–5). They received the word with joy in spite of suffering, imitated Paul and the Lord, and became an example to believers everywhere; their faith became famous (vv. 6–8). Everyone talks of how they turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven, Jesus, who rescues from the coming wrath (vv. 9–10). The chapter is a portrait of genuine conversion.

Setting and background. Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia and a busy port on the great Roman road, the Via Egnatia. Paul, Silas and Timothy came there after being beaten and jailed in Philippi (Acts 16–17). They preached in the synagogue for three Sabbaths, and some Jews and many God-fearing Greeks believed. But jealous Jews started a riot, and the missionaries had to leave by night (Acts 17:1–10). Paul, anxious for the new church, sent Timothy back; Timothy’s good report prompted this letter, written from Corinth around AD 50–51 (3:1–6; Acts 18:5).

Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy. Key words. Silvanus is Silas (Acts 15:40), Paul’s companion in founding the church. No titles: the Thessalonians knew them.

To the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. Church (ekklēsia, assembly): the word for a city’s civic assembly. This assembly lives in God and Christ, not just in Thessalonica. The Father and the Son are named together as the sphere of the church’s life: an early, natural witness to Christ’s deity.

Grace to you and peace. Key words. The shortest of Paul’s greetings.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church was a mere civic club. It was gathered by God, in God.

In a sentence. From Paul, Silas and Timothy, to the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: grace and peace to you.

On a Tuesday. Your church lives in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Thank him for it, and pray for it today.
verseByVerse.note: Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia and a busy port on the Via Egnatia, Rome’s great east–west road. Paul founded the church on his second journey but was soon driven out. Silvanus is the Silas of Acts. Paul probably wrote from Corinth around AD 50, making this one of his earliest letters.

verseByVerse.ref: 1:2–10 – Faith, Love, Hope — and a Church Everyone Was Talking About
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul tells them he never stops thanking God for them, remembering faith that shows itself in action, love that puts in hard work, and hope in Christ that keeps going. He is confident God has chosen them, because the gospel reached them with the Spirit’s power and deep conviction, and they saw how the missionaries lived. They welcomed the message in the middle of persecution, with a joy only the Spirit gives, and so became a pattern for believers across Macedonia and Achaia. People everywhere talk about how they abandoned idols to serve the true God and now wait for his Son, whom God raised, to come from heaven and rescue them from the judgement to come.
verseByVerse.theology:
Election, and How Anyone Could Know

Verse 4 states election flatly and warmly, and verse 5 gives the grounds. Paul claims no private glimpse of the eternal register. He reasons from effect to cause: the gospel arrived among these people with power, the Spirit, and settled conviction, and it produced work, labour and endurance — therefore God had chosen them. The hidden decree becomes visible in time through the effectual call. Peter puts the order exactly: we make our calling and election sure (2 Pet. 1:10) — the election is known through the calling.

Two guards keep this from going wrong. Their faith and love are not the ground of their election — that lies wholly in God — but they are the evidence of it; fruit confirming a root nobody can dig up and inspect. And notice the pastoral use Paul makes of the doctrine. He does not deploy it to sort the congregation or to threaten. He hands it to persecuted people as the one piece of ground that cannot shift: if your standing rested on the firmness of your own decision, a hard enough season could undo it; resting on his choice, it cannot.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Thessalonica was the provincial capital, and its religion was civic rather than private. Trade guilds met at sacrificial meals under patron gods; households kept their own deities; loyalty to Rome was expressed in the imperial cult. To turn from idols was not a change of opinion but resignation from the life of the town, which is precisely why affliction followed (v.6). And the whole thing happened fast: Paul had perhaps a month in the city (Acts 17:2) before a mob forced him out at night, yet within months this church was the pattern held up to older congregations across two provinces.

Now: Verse 3 supplies a test worth running, because faith, love and hope cost nothing to claim. Paul measures each by its output — work, exhaustion, staying put. Ask not whether you have them but whether anything in your week would look different if you did not. And verse 9 gives the useful form of the idol question: since ours are rarely carved, asking whether you own any statues settles nothing. Ask what you serve — what the week is organised around, what you are most afraid of losing, what you would trade sleep and integrity to keep.

verseByVerse.quote: We give thanks to God always for all of you, constantly mentioning you in our prayers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We give thanks to God always for all of you, constantly mentioning you in our prayers,

We give thanks to God always for all of you. Key words. Thanksgiving to God, not to the Thessalonians: their faith is God’s work. Always, for all: no one left out.

Constantly mentioning you in our prayers. Key words. Regular, specific prayer for them by name. Paul prayed for his churches continually.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul prayed every second. It means regular, faithful prayer.

In a sentence. We always thank God for all of you and continually mention you in our prayers.

For worship. Name three believers you know, and thank God for them now.

verseByVerse.quote: remembering before our God and Father your work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
remembering before our God and Father your work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ.

Remembering before our God and Father. Key words. In prayer, Paul recalls what God has done in them.

Your work of faith. Key words. Faith that works: not idle belief, but faith that produces action (James 2:18; Galatians 5:6).

And labor of love. Key words. “Labour” (kopos, toil to weariness). Love that works hard for others, even when exhausted.

And steadfastness of hope. Key words. “Steadfastness” (hypomonē, endurance under pressure). Hope that keeps going under persecution, because it looks to Christ’s return.

In our Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. All three centred on Christ. Faith, love and hope: the triad Paul returns to again and again (5:8; 1 Corinthians 13:13; Colossians 1:4–5). Faith looks back to what Christ has done, love looks around to others, hope looks forward to his coming.

What it does not mean. It does not mean works earn salvation. They are the work that faith produces.

In a sentence. We remember before our God and Father your work produced by faith, your labour prompted by love, and your endurance inspired by hope in our Lord Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. Is your faith working, your love labouring, your hope enduring? Ask God to strengthen all three today.
verseByVerse.note: Faith, love and hope — the triad Paul returns to again and again.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know, brothers loved by God, that he has chosen you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we know, brothers loved by God, that he has chosen you,

For we know, brothers loved by God. Key words. “Loved” (ēgapēmenoi, perfect tense: loved and still loved). The ground of election is God’s love (Deuteronomy 7:7–8; Ephesians 1:4–5).

That he has chosen you. Key words. “Chosen” (eklogē, election, choosing out). God chose them for salvation (2 Thessalonians 2:13). Paul knows this, not by reading God’s secret decree, but by seeing the evidence in their lives (vv. 5–10).

Where Christians differ: can we know who is elect? Some say election is unknowable and therefore irrelevant; others claim to know others’ eternal destiny. Verdict: Election is God’s free choice before the foundation of the world, not based on foreseen faith (Ephesians 1:4; Romans 9:11). We cannot read God’s secret will directly, but election shows itself in its fruits: the gospel received with power and conviction, a turning from idols, faith, love and hope (vv. 3–10; 2 Peter 1:10). So believers may have assurance of their election, and the church may speak of believers as chosen, while leaving final judgement to God (Westminster 3.8).

What it does not mean. It does not mean election makes evangelism unnecessary. Election came to the Thessalonians through preaching (v. 5).

In a sentence. For we know, brothers and sisters loved by God, that he has chosen you,

For worship. If you are in Christ, God loved you and chose you. Bow in wonder and thanks.

verseByVerse.quote: because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction. You know what kind of men we proved to be among you for your sake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction. You know what kind of men we proved to be among you for your sake.

Because our gospel came to you not only in word. Key words. The evidence of election. The gospel came in words: it was preached, with content. But not only words.

But also in power and in the Holy Spirit. Key words. The Spirit made the words effective, changing hearts. Power may include miracles, but mainly the power that converts (Romans 1:16; 1 Corinthians 2:4).

And with full conviction. Key words. “Full conviction” (plērophoria, full assurance). The preachers spoke with conviction, and the hearers received it with conviction.

You know what kind of men we proved to be among you for your sake. Key words. The preachers’ lives backed up their message. Paul will defend his conduct in chapter 2.

What it does not mean. It does not mean words are unimportant. The Spirit works through the word, not apart from it.

In a sentence. because our gospel came to you not simply with words but also with power, with the Holy Spirit and deep conviction. You know how we lived among you for your sake.

On a Tuesday. Pray that when you share the gospel, the Spirit will make your words powerful. And live so your life backs up your words.

verseByVerse.quote: And you became imitators of us and of the Lord, for you received the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit, so that you became an example to all the believers in Macedonia and in Achaia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you became imitators of us and of the Lord, for you received the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit, so that you became an example to all the believers in Macedonia and in Achaia.

And you became imitators of us and of the Lord. Key words. They copied the missionaries, and through them, the Lord himself, especially in suffering.

For you received the word in much affliction. Key words. “Affliction” (thlipsis, pressure, persecution). They believed in the middle of riots and opposition (Acts 17:5–9).

With the joy of the Holy Spirit. Key words. Joy and affliction together. A supernatural joy, given by the Spirit, which persecution could not destroy (Acts 13:52).

So that you became an example to all the believers in Macedonia and in Achaia. Key words. Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece, with Corinth its chief city. “Example” (typos, pattern, model). A young church became a model for others.

What it does not mean. It does not mean joy means the absence of sorrow. It means joy deeper than circumstances.

In a sentence. You became imitators of us and of the Lord, for you welcomed the message in the midst of severe suffering with the joy given by the Holy Spirit. And so you became a model to all the believers in Macedonia and Achaia.

For worship. Ask the Holy Spirit for joy in the middle of your difficulties.
verseByVerse.note: Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece, with Corinth as its capital.

verseByVerse.quote: For not only has the word of the Lord sounded forth from you in Macedonia and Achaia, but your faith in God has gone forth everywhere, so that we need not say anything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For not only has the word of the Lord sounded forth from you in Macedonia and Achaia, but your faith in God has gone forth everywhere, so that we need not say anything.

For not only has the word of the Lord sounded forth from you. Key words. “Sounded forth” (exēcheō, rang out, echoed, like a trumpet or thunder). The gospel rang out from Thessalonica. The busy port and road made it a natural centre for spreading news.

In Macedonia and Achaia. Key words. Throughout Greece.

But your faith in God has gone forth everywhere. Key words. News of their conversion spread far beyond. Changed lives are the best advertisement for the gospel.

So that we need not say anything. Key words. Paul did not need to tell others about them; people already knew.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every person in the world had heard. It means their reputation spread widely.

In a sentence. The Lord’s message rang out from you not only in Macedonia and Achaia; your faith in God has become known everywhere. Therefore we do not need to say anything about it,

On a Tuesday. Let your faith be the kind that others talk about, not for your glory, but so the word of the Lord rings out.

verseByVerse.quote: For they themselves report concerning us the kind of reception we had among you, and how you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For they themselves report concerning us the kind of reception we had among you, and how you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God,

For they themselves report concerning us the kind of reception we had among you. Key words. People everywhere were telling the story of the missionaries’ visit.

And how you turned to God from idols. Key words. Turning “from idols” shows that most of the church were converted pagans, not Jews. Conversion: a decisive turn. To God first, then from idols. Not just giving up idols, but embracing God. Thessalonica had temples to many gods, including the emperor.

To serve the living and true God. Key words. Idols are dead and false; God is living and true (Jeremiah 10:10; Acts 14:15). “Serve” (douleuō, as a slave). They exchanged one master for another, the true one.

What it does not mean. It does not mean modern people have no idols. Anything we trust or love more than God is an idol (Colossians 3:5).

In a sentence. for they themselves report what kind of reception you gave us. They tell how you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God,

For worship. Name an idol you have turned from. Thank God for the living and true God you now serve.
verseByVerse.note: Turning “from idols” shows that most of the church were converted pagans, not Jews.

verseByVerse.quote: and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come.

And to wait for his Son from heaven. Key words. Conversion includes eager expectation of Christ’s return. “Wait” (anamenō, wait expectantly). The second coming is a major theme of this letter (2:19; 3:13; 4:13–18; 5:1–11, 23).

Whom he raised from the dead. Key words. The resurrection proves he is God’s Son and guarantees his return (Acts 17:31).

Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come. Key words. “Delivers” (rhyomai, rescues, present tense: is rescuing). The wrath to come: God’s judgement on sin at the end (Romans 5:9). Jesus rescues believers from it by having borne it himself.

Where Christians differ: wrath and the rapture. Some read deliverance from the wrath to come (here and 5:9) as a promise that believers will be removed from the earth in a secret rapture before a seven-year tribulation. Verdict: The wrath to come is God’s final judgement on the ungodly at the last day (Romans 2:5; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–9). Believers are rescued from it through Christ’s death and resurrection. This does not promise escape from all suffering beforehand; the Thessalonians were already suffering (v. 6; 3:3). Christ will return once, visibly, to raise the dead, rescue his people and judge the world. There is no secret rapture.

What it does not mean. It does not mean waiting is passive. They waited by serving (v. 9).

In a sentence. and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead: Jesus, who rescues us from the coming wrath.

On a Tuesday. Live today as one waiting for Jesus from heaven. Serve while you wait.

2.title: A Nursing Mother and a Urging Father
2.overview:
After Paul’s hurried departure, someone was evidently saying he had been just another travelling religious salesman: a flatterer after money and fame who ran when it got hard. Paul answers by appealing to what the Thessalonians saw with their own eyes. He came still bruised from Philippi and preached anyway. He did not flatter, cheat or seek praise, though as an apostle he could have demanded support. He was gentle as a nursing mother and urged them on like a father, and he worked night and day at his trade so as not to burden anyone.

He thanks God that they received his message as what it really is, God’s word, which is now at work in them, even though it brought persecution from their own countrymen, as the Judean churches suffered from theirs. Then his grief shows: he was “orphaned” from them, Satan blocked his return, yet they are his hope, joy and crown when the Lord Jesus comes.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul reminds them how the mission began. Fresh from being mistreated in Philippi, the missionaries still spoke boldly. Their appeal came from no error, impure motive or trickery; entrusted with the gospel by God, they aimed to please him, not people. They used no flattery, sought no profit and demanded no honour, though as apostles they could have. Instead they were gentle among them like a nursing mother, sharing not only the gospel but their own lives. They worked night and day so as not to be a burden, lived holy and blameless lives among them, and like a father urged each one to live worthily of God, who calls them into his kingdom and glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Minister as Steward, Not Owner

The governing idea of the passage is in verse 4: entrusted with the gospel. The word is used of a deposit placed in someone's keeping. It is not Paul's gospel, as though he had devised it — he is a courier carrying what belongs to another, and a courier does not edit the parcel. The Reformed tradition has always insisted the minister stands under the word rather than over it: a steward, never an entrepreneur.

Notice that Paul uses the assayer's word dokimazo twice in one sentence. He has been tested and approved; and he speaks before the God who goes on testing hearts. The examination is continuous, which is why the sentence lands where it does — not to please man, but to please God. This is not indifference to people; Paul has just described treating them with a nursing mother's tenderness. It is a question of whose verdict he is working for, and the two audiences pull apart at exactly the point where the true thing and the popular thing separate.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The circuit Paul travelled was worked by professional lecturers and religious salesmen who lived on their rhetoric, took what they could get, and moved on. The quickest way to destroy a young church was to persuade it that its founder had been one of them. So Paul answers with what could be checked: they had watched him arrive injured and preach anyway, and they had watched him at a leatherworker's bench before dawn and after dark so that none of them would have to pay for him.

Now: Verse 6 is the sharpest line for anyone holding office. Paul had the right to be supported and honoured, defends that right vigorously elsewhere (1 Cor 9:4-14), and declined to press it. The question in ministry — as in any relationship where one party holds the power — is almost never whether you have a right. Usually you do. It is what you intend to do with it. And verse 9 needs its guard: Paul is not ruling out paid ministry, which he explicitly upholds (1 Cor 9:14; and 5:12 below). He waived a fair claim in one place for one reason, so that nothing about money could stand between these people and the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: For you yourselves know, brothers, that our coming to you was not in vain. But though we had already suffered and been shamefully treated at Philippi, as you know, we had boldness in our God to declare to you the gospel of God in the midst of much conflict.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you yourselves know, brothers, that our coming to you was not in vain. But though we had already suffered and been shamefully treated at Philippi, as you know, we had boldness in our God to declare to you the gospel of God in the midst of much conflict.

Meaning first. 1 Thessalonians 2 is Paul’s defence of his ministry in Thessalonica. After his sudden departure, opponents seem to have said he was just another travelling preacher, in it for money or fame, who abandoned his converts at the first sign of trouble. Paul reminds them what they saw. He preached boldly despite suffering; his message was not from error, impurity or trickery; he spoke to please God, not people; he never used flattery or greed, but was gentle like a nursing mother and shared his very life with them; he worked night and day to support himself; and he exhorted them like a father to live worthy of God (vv. 1–12). He thanks God that they received his message as what it truly is, the word of God, and that they endured persecution from their own people as the Judean churches had (vv. 13–16). Finally he explains that his absence was not by choice: he longed to see them, but Satan blocked the way. They are his hope, joy and crown at Christ’s coming (vv. 17–20). The chapter is a portrait of a true pastor.

For you yourselves know, brothers, that our coming to you was not in vain. Key words. “In vain” (kenē, empty). Not hollow or fruitless. The church itself was proof.

But though we had already suffered and been shamefully treated at Philippi, as you know. Key words. At Philippi Paul and Silas had been beaten and jailed just before coming to Thessalonica (Acts 16:22–24). Shamefully treated: stripped and flogged in public, Roman citizens though they were.

We had boldness in our God to declare to you the gospel of God. Key words. “Boldness” (parrēsiazomai, spoke freely, courageously). In our God: the courage came from God. Bruised and sore, they preached anyway.

In the midst of much conflict. Key words. “Conflict” (agōn, struggle, contest). Opposition in Thessalonica too (Acts 17:5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul felt no fear. It means God gave courage greater than fear.

In a sentence. You know, brothers and sisters, that our visit to you was not without results. We had previously suffered and been treated outrageously in Philippi, as you know, but with the help of our God we dared to tell you his gospel in the face of strong opposition.

On a Tuesday. If you have been hurt for your faith, ask God for boldness to keep speaking.
verseByVerse.note: At Philippi Paul and Silas had been beaten and jailed just before they came to Thessalonica.

verseByVerse.quote: For our appeal does not spring from error or impurity or any attempt to deceive, but just as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel, so we speak, not to please man, but to please God who tests our hearts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For our appeal does not spring from error or impurity or any attempt to deceive, but just as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel, so we speak, not to please man, but to please God who tests our hearts.

For our appeal does not spring from error. Key words. “Appeal” (paraklēsis, exhortation, preaching). Not from error: the message is true.

Or impurity. Key words. Not from impure motives. Some pagan cults involved sexual immorality; some travelling teachers sought sexual favours.

Or any attempt to deceive. Key words. “Deceive” (dolos, bait, trickery). No manipulation.

But just as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel. Key words. “Approved” (dokimazō, tested and approved). God tested them and entrusted them with the gospel, as a steward (1 Corinthians 4:1–2).

So we speak, not to please man, but to please God who tests our hearts. Key words. God examines motives (Jeremiah 11:20; Psalm 139:23). The preacher answers to him, not to the audience (Galatians 1:10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul did not care about his hearers. He cared deeply (v. 8). But his aim was to please God.

In a sentence. For the appeal we make does not spring from error or impure motives, nor are we trying to trick you. On the contrary, we speak as those approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel. We are not trying to please people but God, who tests our hearts.

For worship. Ask God to test your heart and purify your motives in serving him.

verseByVerse.quote: For we never came with words of flattery, as you know, nor with a pretext for greed—God is witness. Nor did we seek glory from people, whether from you or from others, though we could have made demands as apostles of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we never came with words of flattery, as you know, nor with a pretext for greed—God is witness. Nor did we seek glory from people, whether from you or from others, though we could have made demands as apostles of Christ.

For we never came with words of flattery, as you know. Key words. Flattery tells people what they want to hear to win them. Paul did not.

Nor with a pretext for greed—God is witness. Key words. “Pretext” (prophasis, a mask). No hidden money motive. Only God could witness the heart, so Paul calls on him.

Nor did we seek glory from people, whether from you or from others. Key words. Not seeking fame or honour.

Though we could have made demands as apostles of Christ. Key words. Literally, though we could have been a weight, a burden, or could have stood on our dignity. They had a right to support and honour (1 Corinthians 9:4–6), but did not insist.

What it does not mean. It does not mean encouragement is flattery. Paul encouraged them often. Flattery is insincere praise to gain advantage.

In a sentence. You know we never used flattery, nor did we put on a mask to cover up greed; God is our witness. We were not looking for praise from people, not from you or anyone else, even though as apostles of Christ we could have asserted our authority.

On a Tuesday. Do you flatter people to win them? Speak honestly and kindly instead.

verseByVerse.quote: But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother taking care of her own children. So, being affectionately desirous of you, we were ready to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own selves, because you had become very dear to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother taking care of her own children. So, being affectionately desirous of you, we were ready to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own selves, because you had become very dear to us.

But we were gentle among you. Key words. “Gentle” (ēpioi). Some manuscripts read “infants” (nēpioi), as the ESV notes: one letter different. Either way, the opposite of domineering.

Like a nursing mother taking care of her own children. Key words. “Taking care” (thalpō, cherishing, keeping warm, as a bird warms its eggs). Her own children: the tenderness a mother feels for her own. A surprising picture of apostolic ministry: tender, nourishing, self-giving.

So, being affectionately desirous of you. Key words. “Affectionately desirous” (homeiromai, yearning for, a rare tender word).

We were ready to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own selves. Key words. “Selves” (psychai, lives, souls). Not just the message, but their lives: time, energy, hearts. Gospel ministry is life-on-life.

Because you had become very dear to us. Key words. Love for people, not just for the work.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministry is all softness. Paul also exhorted like a father (v. 11). Gentleness and strength together.

In a sentence. Instead, we were like young children among you. Just as a nursing mother cares for her children, so we cared for you. Because we loved you so much, we were delighted to share with you not only the gospel of God but our lives as well.

For worship. Thank God for people who shared their lives with you as well as the gospel. Share yours with someone.

verseByVerse.quote: For you remember, brothers, our labor and toil: we worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you, while we proclaimed to you the gospel of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you remember, brothers, our labor and toil: we worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you, while we proclaimed to you the gospel of God.

For you remember, brothers, our labor and toil. Key words. “Labour and toil” (kopos kai mochthos, hard work and hardship).

We worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you. Key words. Paul supported himself by his trade: he was a tentmaker, working with leather (Acts 18:3; 20:34). Night and day: starting before dawn. He refused to be a financial burden on a poor young church, and to give any ground for the charge of greed.

While we proclaimed to you the gospel of God. Key words. Preaching while working, perhaps in the workshop itself.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers should never be paid. Paul defended the right elsewhere (1 Corinthians 9:14). He chose not to use it here.

In a sentence. Surely you remember, brothers and sisters, our toil and hardship; we worked night and day in order not to be a burden to anyone while we preached the gospel of God to you.

On a Tuesday. Your ordinary work can support gospel witness. Let your workplace be a place where you share Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Paul supported himself by his trade — he was a tentmaker.

verseByVerse.quote: You are witnesses, and God also, how holy and righteous and blameless was our conduct toward you believers. For you know how, like a father with his children, we exhorted each one of you and encouraged you and charged you to walk in a manner worthy of God, who calls you into his own kingdom and glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are witnesses, and God also, how holy and righteous and blameless was our conduct toward you believers. For you know how, like a father with his children, we exhorted each one of you and encouraged you and charged you to walk in a manner worthy of God, who calls you into his own kingdom and glory.

You are witnesses, and God also, how holy and righteous and blameless was our conduct toward you believers. Key words. Three words: holy (devoted to God), righteous (just toward people), blameless (no ground for accusation). Both they and God can testify.

For you know how, like a father with his children. Key words. Now a father picture, alongside the mother of verse 7. Fathers taught and trained their children.

We exhorted each one of you. Key words. Each one: personal attention, not just public preaching (Acts 20:20).

And encouraged you and charged you. Key words. Exhorted (parakaleō, urged), encouraged (paramytheomai, comforted), charged (martyromai, solemnly insisted). Three tones of fatherly guidance.

To walk in a manner worthy of God. Key words. Live in a way that fits who God is and what he has done.

Who calls you into his own kingdom and glory. Key words. Present tense: God keeps calling them. His kingdom and glory: their destiny. Live worthy of where you are going.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul claimed sinlessness. It means his conduct among them was above reproach.

In a sentence. You are witnesses, and so is God, of how holy, righteous and blameless we were among you who believed. For you know that we dealt with each of you as a father deals with his own children, encouraging, comforting and urging you to live lives worthy of God, who calls you into his kingdom and glory.

For worship. God is calling you into his kingdom and glory. Ask him to help you live worthy of that call today.

verseByVerse.ref: 2:13–16 – How They Received the Word — and What It Cost
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul thanks God that they received the message not as a human idea but as what it truly is, God’s word, which is at work in those who believe. They have suffered from their own people just as the churches in Judea suffered from theirs. Paul speaks severely of those who killed the Lord and the prophets, drove out the apostles, and try to stop the gospel reaching the Gentiles, filling up the measure of their sins, with God’s wrath coming upon them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Scripture as God's Own Speech

Verse 13 is one of the clearest statements in the New Testament of what Scripture is: received as human opinion the word does nothing; received as what it really is, the word of God, it goes to work (energeitai). Paul is describing not two kinds of Bible but two kinds of hearing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Verses 15–16 have been misused across the centuries. Paul, a Jew who insists God has not rejected his people (Rom 9:3; 11:1), names a target by its actions — those who killed Jesus and the prophets and were blocking the mission to the Gentiles — in the insider language of covenant rebuke.

Now: The wrath of verse 16 must be read beside 1:10, where wrath is what Jesus delivers people from — Paul himself included. A sober warning is never a licence for contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: And we also thank God constantly for this, that when you received the word of God, which you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God, which is at work in you believers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we also thank God constantly for this, that when you received the word of God, which you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God, which is at work in you believers.

And we also thank God constantly for this. Key words. Another thanksgiving.

That when you received the word of God, which you heard from us. Key words. They heard human preachers speaking.

You accepted it not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God. Key words. The apostolic message was God’s word through human messengers. “Received” (paralambanō, outward hearing) and “accepted” (dechomai, welcomed inwardly). They welcomed it as God speaking.

Which is at work in you believers. Key words. “At work” (energeō). God’s word is not dead letters but living power, working in those who believe it (Hebrews 4:12; Isaiah 55:11).

Where Christians differ: is Scripture the word of God? Some say the Bible contains or becomes the word of God, or is merely human testimony. Verdict: The apostles’ message, now written in Scripture, is what it really is: the word of God, not merely the words of men, though spoken through men. Scripture is God-breathed and authoritative in all it affirms (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21; Westminster 1.4). Its authority does not depend on human acceptance; it is God’s word whether received or not, and it works in those who believe.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every preacher’s words are God’s word. Only as preaching faithfully conveys Scripture does it carry God’s authority.

In a sentence. And we also thank God continually because, when you received the word of God, which you heard from us, you accepted it not as a human word, but as it actually is, the word of God, which is indeed at work in you who believe.

On a Tuesday. When you read Scripture today, receive it as God speaking to you. Let it work in you.

verseByVerse.quote: For you, brothers, became imitators of the churches of God in Christ Jesus that are in Judea. For you suffered the same things from your own countrymen as they did from the Jews,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you, brothers, became imitators of the churches of God in Christ Jesus that are in Judea. For you suffered the same things from your own countrymen as they did from the Jews,

For you, brothers, became imitators of the churches of God in Christ Jesus that are in Judea. Key words. The proof that the word was at work: they endured persecution like the first churches.

For you suffered the same things from your own countrymen. Key words. Fellow Thessalonians, Gentiles, stirred up by some Jews (Acts 17:5–9).

As they did from the Jews. Key words. The Judean churches suffered from Jewish authorities (Acts 8:1–3; 12:1–3). Suffering for Christ is the shared experience of the whole church.

What it does not mean. It does not mean persecution proves a church true. But faithful churches should expect it (2 Timothy 3:12).

In a sentence. For you, brothers and sisters, became imitators of God’s churches in Judea, which are in Christ Jesus: you suffered from your own people the same things those churches suffered from the Jews

For worship. Pray for churches suffering persecution from their own countrymen today.

verseByVerse.quote: who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets, and drove us out, and displease God and oppose all mankind by hindering us from speaking to the Gentiles that they might be saved—so as always to fill up the measure of their sins. But wrath has come upon them at last!
verseByVerse.commentary:
who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets, and drove us out, and displease God and oppose all mankind by hindering us from speaking to the Gentiles that they might be saved—so as always to fill up the measure of their sins. But wrath has come upon them at last!

Who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets. Key words. The Jewish leaders who rejected Christ, following a long pattern of killing prophets (Matthew 23:29–37; Acts 7:52).

And drove us out. Key words. From Thessalonica and elsewhere (Acts 17:5–10, 13).

And displease God and oppose all mankind. Key words. Opposing the gospel is opposing God and the good of all people.

By hindering us from speaking to the Gentiles that they might be saved. Key words. Their chief sin: trying to stop Gentiles hearing the gospel.

So as always to fill up the measure of their sins. Key words. As God waited until the Amorites’ sin was complete (Genesis 15:16), so these opponents were filling up their sins to the point of judgement (Matthew 23:32).

But wrath has come upon them at last! Key words. God’s judgement is certain, perhaps already beginning: within twenty years, Jerusalem would be destroyed (AD 70). “At last” may mean fully, or to the end.

Where Christians differ: is this anti-Jewish? Some say this passage is anti-Semitic, or that it was not written by Paul. Verdict: Paul, himself a Jew, is speaking of those who opposed the gospel, not of the Jewish people as a whole. He loved his people deeply and longed for their salvation (Romans 9:1–5; 10:1), and many of the first believers were Jews. His language echoes Jesus and the prophets, who spoke similarly to Israel. Christians must never use this passage to justify hatred of Jews, which is a terrible sin that has stained church history.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all Jews are under wrath, or that Jews alone killed Jesus. Gentiles shared in it (Acts 4:27), and our sins put him there.

In a sentence. who killed the Lord Jesus and the prophets and also drove us out. They displease God and are hostile to everyone in their effort to keep us from speaking to the Gentiles so that they may be saved. In this way they always heap up their sins to the limit. The wrath of God has come upon them at last.

On a Tuesday. Pray for Jewish people to come to faith in Jesus their Messiah. And pray for opponents of the gospel to be saved, as Paul was.
verseByVerse.note: Paul, himself a Jew, is speaking of those who opposed the gospel, as he had once done — not of every Jewish person.

parallels.desc: the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete

verseByVerse.ref: 2:17–20 – Orphaned From Them, and What He Expects to Hold
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Torn away from them for a short time, absent in body but not in heart, Paul longed to see them again and tried more than once to return, but Satan blocked the way. They are his hope, joy and crown of boasting before the Lord Jesus at his coming; they are his glory and joy.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Coming, and the Pastor's Wreath

Verse 19 brings in parousia, the word for a sovereign's state visit, and pictures Paul at the King's arrival holding nothing but a wreath made of people. The reward of pastoral work is not the admiration of the present age but the sight, on that day, of people standing before Jesus because the gospel was faithfully preached and patiently tended.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul read his blocked return not as bad luck or as God saying no but as the work of an enemy — and the enemy did not win: Timothy went in his place, and this letter exists because Paul could not come.

Now: On the last day, is what you expect to hold up a record of what you achieved, or people who are standing there because of it?

verseByVerse.quote: But since we were torn away from you, brothers, for a short time, in person not in heart, we endeavored the more eagerly and with great desire to see you face to face, because we wanted to come to you—I, Paul, again and again—but Satan hindered us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But since we were torn away from you, brothers, for a short time, in person not in heart, we endeavored the more eagerly and with great desire to see you face to face, because we wanted to come to you—I, Paul, again and again—but Satan hindered us.

But since we were torn away from you, brothers, for a short time. Key words. “Torn away” (aporphanizō, orphaned, bereaved). Paul felt like a parent separated from his children, or an orphan. His departure was forced (Acts 17:10).

In person not in heart. Key words. Absent in body, present in love.

We endeavored the more eagerly and with great desire to see you face to face. Key words. Strong words of longing. Opponents said he did not care; he cared intensely.

Because we wanted to come to you—I, Paul, again and again. Key words. Paul personally tried more than once.

But Satan hindered us. Key words. “Hindered” (enkoptō, cut in, blocked, as breaking up a road). Satan used circumstances, perhaps the bond Jason gave (Acts 17:9), or continued hostility. Paul sees spiritual warfare behind events.

Where Christians differ: Satan’s power over circumstances. Some blame Satan for every difficulty; others ignore him. Verdict: Satan is real and does oppose God’s work, sometimes through circumstances (Job 1–2; 2 Corinthians 12:7). But he acts only within the limits God permits, and God overrules even his opposition for good (Romans 8:28). Elsewhere Paul says God or the Spirit prevented him from going somewhere (Acts 16:6–7). Discernment is needed, and in every case we trust God’s sovereign providence (Westminster 5.4).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Satan is as strong as God. He is a defeated foe on a leash.

In a sentence. But, brothers and sisters, when we were orphaned by being separated from you for a short time (in person, not in thought), out of our intense longing we made every effort to see you. For we wanted to come to you; certainly Paul did, again and again, but Satan blocked our way.

For worship. When your good plans are blocked, bring it to God. He rules even over Satan’s opposition.

verseByVerse.quote: For what is our hope or joy or crown of boasting before our Lord Jesus at his coming? Is it not you? For you are our glory and joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what is our hope or joy or crown of boasting before our Lord Jesus at his coming? Is it not you? For you are our glory and joy.

For what is our hope or joy or crown of boasting. Key words. “Crown” (stephanos, victor’s wreath). Crown of boasting: the prize Paul will rejoice in.

Before our Lord Jesus at his coming? Key words. “Coming” (parousia, arrival, presence): the word used for the visit of a king or emperor. The first use in Paul of this term for Christ’s return.

Is it not you? For you are our glory and joy. Key words. The Thessalonians themselves will be Paul’s reward. On the last day, seeing them standing in Christ will be his joy (Philippians 4:1). The best reward of ministry is people.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s salvation depended on them. It means they will be the joy and fruit of his labour.

In a sentence. For what is our hope, our joy, or the crown in which we will glory in the presence of our Lord Jesus when he comes? Is it not you? Indeed, you are our glory and joy.

On a Tuesday. Who will be your joy when Jesus comes? Invest in people today.

3.title: Standing Firm in the Lord
3.overview:
Paul could not bear not knowing whether the young church had survived persecution. So he stayed alone in Athens and sent Timothy back to strengthen them, reminding them that suffering was what they had been warned to expect, and fearing that the tempter had talked them out of the faith. Now Timothy has returned with good news: their faith and love are holding, and they long to see Paul as he longs to see them.

Paul says, “now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord.” He cannot thank God enough, and prays night and day to see them and fill the gaps in their teaching. The chapter ends with a prayer that God will clear his road to them, make their love overflow to everyone, and strengthen their hearts to be blameless in holiness when Jesus comes with all his holy ones.

verseByVerse.ref: 3:1–5 – Timothy Sent, and Suffering as a Posting
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Unable to bear the silence any longer, Paul stayed alone in Athens and sent Timothy, his fellow worker, to strengthen and encourage them, so that no one would be shaken by their troubles. Paul had warned them that suffering was part of the Christian calling, and it had come. He sent Timothy for fear that the tempter had shaken their faith and his work had been wasted.
verseByVerse.theology:
Affliction as Appointment, Not Accident

The key word in verse 3 is keimetha — we are laid, set in place, appointed. It is the language of a stone set in a foundation or a sentry posted, and Paul uses the same root of himself in prison, put there for the defence of the gospel (Phil 1:16). Suffering for the gospel is not something that slipped past God's attention; it is a placement.

That is the pastoral logic, and it needs stating carefully. What steadies a shaken believer is not the promise that the trouble will stop but the assurance that the trouble is not a mistake. If hardship means the plan has gone wrong, every difficult week is evidence against the faith. If hardship is where God has laid you, the difficult week proves only that you are where he put you. The Reformed tradition has held this consistently: God governs all things, his people's afflictions included, and such suffering is purposeful — producing endurance, character and hope (Rom 5:3-4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul feared not that persecution would smash this church but that it would coax them out of it (v.3) — faith is usually lost by erosion, not by renunciation.

Now: Honest preparation for hardship is a form of pastoral care, and its absence is a cruelty disguised as encouragement (v.4).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore when we could bear it no longer, we were willing to be left behind at Athens alone, and we sent Timothy, our brother and God's coworker in the gospel of Christ, to establish and exhort you in your faith,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore when we could bear it no longer, we were willing to be left behind at Athens alone, and we sent Timothy, our brother and God’s coworker in the gospel of Christ, to establish and exhort you in your faith,

Meaning first. 1 Thessalonians 3 shows a pastor’s heart in anxiety and relief. Unable to bear not knowing how the young church was doing under persecution, Paul stayed alone in Athens and sent Timothy to strengthen them, reminding them that suffering was to be expected and fearing that the tempter had shaken them (vv. 1–5). Then Timothy returned with wonderful news of their faith and love and their longing to see Paul. Paul was comforted in his own troubles: now we really live, if you stand firm in the Lord (vv. 6–8). He overflows with thanks and prays night and day to see them again and supply what is lacking in their faith (vv. 9–10). The chapter ends with a prayer: that God would open the way for Paul to come, make their love increase, and establish their hearts blameless in holiness at the coming of the Lord Jesus with all his saints (vv. 11–13).

Therefore when we could bear it no longer. Key words. “Bear” (stegō, endure, hold in). Paul’s concern became unbearable.

We were willing to be left behind at Athens alone. Key words. Paul went from Berea to Athens (Acts 17:15–34). “Left behind” (kataleipō, abandoned): a costly sacrifice. In a hostile, idol-filled city, he chose to be alone so that they could be helped.

And we sent Timothy, our brother and God’s coworker in the gospel of Christ. Key words. High praise: God’s fellow worker. Some manuscripts read “God’s servant,” as the ESV notes. Timothy was young but trusted.

To establish and exhort you in your faith. Key words. “Establish” (stērizō, strengthen, make firm, like propping up a building). “Exhort” (parakaleō, encourage). New believers need follow-up care.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul doubted God. He knew new believers under pressure need support.

In a sentence. So when we could stand it no longer, we thought it best to be left by ourselves in Athens. We sent Timothy, who is our brother and co-worker in God’s service in spreading the gospel of Christ, to strengthen and encourage you in your faith,

On a Tuesday. Who is a young or struggling believer you could help strengthen this week? Go, call or write.

verseByVerse.quote: that no one be moved by these afflictions. For you yourselves know that we are destined for this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
that no one be moved by these afflictions. For you yourselves know that we are destined for this.

That no one be moved by these afflictions. Key words. “Moved” (sainō, shaken, or perhaps fawned upon, lured away). Persecution can shake faith, or tempt people to compromise to escape it.

For you yourselves know that we are destined for this. Key words. “Destined” (keimai, appointed, set). Suffering is part of God’s appointment for his people (Acts 14:22; 2 Timothy 3:12; John 16:33). Not a sign that God has abandoned them, but part of his plan. Knowing this in advance protects from shock.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God delights in his people’s pain. It means he uses it for their good and his glory (Romans 8:28; 1 Peter 1:6–7).

In a sentence. so that no one would be unsettled by these trials. For you know quite well that we are destined for them.

For worship. If you are suffering, it is not a sign God has forgotten you. Trust him in it.

verseByVerse.quote: For when we were with you, we kept telling you beforehand that we were to suffer affliction, just as it has come to pass, and just as you know. For this reason, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to learn about your faith, for fear that somehow the tempter had tempted you and our labor would be in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For when we were with you, we kept telling you beforehand that we were to suffer affliction, just as it has come to pass, and just as you know. For this reason, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to learn about your faith, for fear that somehow the tempter had tempted you and our labor would be in vain.

For when we were with you, we kept telling you beforehand that we were to suffer affliction. Key words. Paul did not promise an easy life. He warned new converts to expect trouble. Honest evangelism counts the cost (Luke 14:28).

Just as it has come to pass, and just as you know. Key words. The warnings came true.

For this reason, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to learn about your faith. Key words. Paul’s personal anxiety (“I”).

For fear that somehow the tempter had tempted you. Key words. The tempter is Satan (Matthew 4:3). He uses suffering to tempt believers to give up.

And our labor would be in vain. Key words. If they fell away, Paul’s work would have been empty.

What it does not mean. It does not mean true believers can be lost. Paul feared that their faith might prove false, which would show his labour fruitless. Timothy’s report proved it genuine.

In a sentence. In fact, when we were with you, we kept telling you that we would be persecuted. And it turned out that way, as you well know. For this reason, when Paul could stand it no longer, he sent to find out about your faith. He was afraid that in some way the tempter had tempted you and that our labours might have been in vain.

On a Tuesday. When you share the gospel, be honest about the cost. And pray for those under pressure to give up.

verseByVerse.ref: 3:6–13 – The News From Home, and a Prayer for Love
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Timothy has now come back with good news of their faith and love, and their warm memories and longing to see Paul. That news has comforted him in his own distress; it is like new life to him to know they stand firm in the Lord. He cannot thank God enough for the joy they bring him, and he prays earnestly to see them again and supply what their faith still lacks. He prays that God will open the way, that the Lord will make their love for one another and for everyone overflow, and that he will strengthen their hearts to be blameless in holiness before God at the coming of the Lord Jesus with all his holy ones.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Persons, One Verb

In verse 11 Paul names the Father and the Lord Jesus as two subjects and gives them one singular verb — the highest view of Christ, already present in the ordinary shape of a man's prayers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What was lacking in their faith (v.10) was not sincerity but completeness — the teaching Paul never got to give.

Now: Paul prays that a persecuted church would overflow in love not only for one another but ‘for all’ (v.12) — the very population making its life hard.

verseByVerse.quote: But now that Timothy has come to us from you, and has brought us the good news of your faith and love and reported that you always remember us kindly and long to see us, as we long to see you— for this reason, brothers, in all our distress and affliction we have been comforted about you through your faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now that Timothy has come to us from you, and has brought us the good news of your faith and love and reported that you always remember us kindly and long to see us, as we long to see you—for this reason, brothers, in all our distress and affliction we have been comforted about you through your faith.

But now that Timothy has come to us from you. Key words. Timothy rejoined Paul in Corinth (Acts 18:5).

And has brought us the good news of your faith and love. Key words. “Brought good news” (euangelizomai, the gospel word). The report was itself like a gospel to Paul. Faith and love: their relationship to God and to others.

And reported that you always remember us kindly and long to see us, as we long to see you. Key words. The slanders had not turned them against Paul.

For this reason, brothers, in all our distress and affliction we have been comforted about you through your faith. Key words. Paul was suffering in Corinth too. Their faith comforted him. Believers comfort one another by standing firm.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s comfort depended only on them. It came from God, through them (2 Corinthians 7:6).

In a sentence. But Timothy has just now come to us from you and has brought good news about your faith and love. He has told us that you always have pleasant memories of us and that you long to see us, just as we also long to see you. Therefore, brothers and sisters, in all our distress and persecution we were encouraged about you because of your faith.

For worship. Thank God for good news of others’ faith. Your faithfulness might be someone else’s comfort.

verseByVerse.quote: For now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord.

For now we live. Key words. Paul feels alive again, renewed. Their faithfulness brings him life.

If you are standing fast in the Lord. Key words. “Standing fast” (stēkō, standing firm). In the Lord: their strength is in him. The “if” is also a gentle encouragement to keep standing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s spiritual life depended on them. It expresses how deeply his joy was bound up with them.

In a sentence. For now we really live, since you are standing firm in the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Stand firm in the Lord today. Others are encouraged by it.

verseByVerse.quote: For what thanksgiving can we return to God for you, for all the joy that we feel for your sake before our God, as we pray most earnestly night and day that we may see you face to face and supply what is lacking in your faith?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what thanksgiving can we return to God for you, for all the joy that we feel for your sake before our God, as we pray most earnestly night and day that we may see you face to face and supply what is lacking in your faith?

For what thanksgiving can we return to God for you. Key words. Paul cannot thank God enough. Their faith is God’s work.

For all the joy that we feel for your sake before our God. Key words. Joy in God’s presence.

As we pray most earnestly night and day. Key words. “Most earnestly” (hyperekperissou, superabundantly, beyond measure). Intense, persistent prayer.

That we may see you face to face. Key words. Letters are not enough. He longs to be with them.

And supply what is lacking in your faith? Key words. “Supply” (katartizō, complete, mend, equip). Their faith was real but young. They needed more teaching, which chapters 4–5 begin to give: on holiness, love, and Christ’s return.

What it does not mean. It does not mean their faith was defective. It means it was growing and needed more instruction.

In a sentence. How can we thank God enough for you in return for all the joy we have in the presence of our God because of you? Night and day we pray most earnestly that we may see you again and supply what is lacking in your faith.

For worship. Thank God for the believers who bring you joy. Pray for them to grow.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you,

Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus. Key words. A prayer addressed to the Father and the Son together.

Direct our way to you. Key words. “Direct” (kateuthynō, make straight, clear the path). Satan had blocked the way (2:18); God can open it. Remarkably, the verb is singular in Greek, though it has two subjects: God and Father, and our Lord Jesus. The Father and the Son act as one. An early witness to the unity of the Father and the Son, and so to Christ’s deity.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Father and the Son are one person. They are distinct persons who act as one God.

In a sentence. Now may our God and Father himself and our Lord Jesus clear the way for us to come to you.

On a Tuesday. Ask God to direct your way today. He can clear any obstacle.

verseByVerse.quote: and may the Lord make you increase and abound in love for one another and for all, as we do for you, so that he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and may the Lord make you increase and abound in love for one another and for all, as we do for you, so that he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.

And may the Lord make you increase and abound in love. Key words. Love grows as the Lord makes it grow. “Increase” (pleonazō) and “abound” (perisseuō, overflow). A flood of love.

For one another and for all. Key words. Fellow believers first, and also all people, including persecutors.

As we do for you. Key words. Paul’s love is the model.

So that he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness. Key words. Love leads to holiness. “Establish” (stērizō, strengthen). Blameless: without just accusation.

Before our God and Father. Key words. In his presence, at the judgement.

At the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints. Key words. Christ’s return (parousia). His saints (holy ones): either angels, who accompany him (Matthew 25:31; Zechariah 14:5), or believers who have died, whom he brings with him (4:14), or both.

Where Christians differ: coming for his saints, or with them? Some dispensationalists distinguish Christ coming for his saints (a secret rapture) from coming with his saints (seven years later). Verdict: Paul describes one coming, at which Christ brings the souls of departed believers with him, raises their bodies, gathers the living, and judges the world (4:14–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). He comes both for and with his saints in a single, visible, glorious return. There is no secret rapture.

What it does not mean. It does not mean blamelessness is achieved by us alone. The Lord establishes it.

In a sentence. May the Lord make your love increase and overflow for each other and for everyone else, just as ours does for you. May he strengthen your hearts so that you will be blameless and holy in the presence of our God and Father when our Lord Jesus comes with all his holy ones.

For worship. Pray this prayer for your church: overflowing love, and hearts established in holiness for Christ’s coming.

parallels.desc: the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him
